This issue is likely caused by the persistent vTPM state not being correctly retained across VM shutdown/start cycles in Proj. Bitlocker relies on the TPM state to remain unchanged; if the vTPM state is lost or reset, Bitlocker will prompt for the recovery key on every boot. Proj uses backend storage (PVCs) to persist vTPM state, and this mechanism depends on the correct creation, binding, and mounting of the backend storage PVC for each VM with persistent TPM enabled. Any misconfiguration, permission issue, or PVC lifecycle problem can result in vTPM state loss, which matches your symptoms. This is a key difference from direct libvirt/qemu setups, where the state is managed on a stable host path and such issues are less likely to occur.

There are no open or closed issues or documentation entries describing this exact Bitlocker/vTPM problem in Proj v1.5.0, but recent code and documentation confirm that persistent vTPM is managed via backend storage PVCs and that the `VMPersistentState` feature gate is required for this to work correctly. Ongoing improvements in this area have addressed related bugs, especially around migration and backend storage handling, but not this specific scenario yet [[docs](https://host-215.example/user-guide/compute/persistent_tpm_and_uefi_state/)].

To troubleshoot, check that the backend storage PVC for the VM is present, bound, and mounted in the VM pod after shutdown/start. Review logs from the virt-launcher and virt-handler pods for errors or warnings related to vTPM or backend storage during the VM lifecycle. Issues with PVC attach/detach, mount, or permissions are common culprits. If the PVC is missing or not mounted, or if there are related errors in the logs, this would explain the Bitlocker recovery prompt.

If everything appears correct with the PVC and logs, but the issue persists, it may be a subtle bug or edge case in Proj's vTPM state management. In that case, gathering detailed logs and environment information will be important for further diagnosis or escalation.

**What happened**:
When I tried to resize an encrypted PVC online, I encountered the problem of "unable to execute QEMU command 'block_resize': Cannot grow device files'". After testing, it was found that the encrypted PVC in LUKS format has a part of the unencrypted header space, so blockresize will fail.

", "closed_by": null, "comments": [{"author": "person-4497d9f9", "body": "<!-- Answer -->
This happens because LUKS encryption adds an unencrypted header at the start of the disk, so the actual usable space for the VM is less than the PVC size. Proj does not account for this header when issuing QEMU block_resize commands—the resize request is passed as-is, which causes the operation to fail if you try to resize to the full PVC size including the header. There is no built-in workaround or automatic adjustment for this in Proj; you need to manually subtract the LUKS header size from your resize request to avoid the error. This limitation is consistent with how Proj and CDI handle block volumes—they do not expect or handle overhead for block devices like LUKS headers during resizing or migration, and the toleration settings only apply to filesystem volumes, not block volumes. Manual adjustment for the header is currently the only way to avoid block_resize failures with encrypted PVCs [(reference)](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/issues/69572).

This is expected behavior: Proj's node-labeller component adds many CPU feature labels to all targeted nodes (like `cpu_feature_node_proj_io_ibpb`, `ibrs`, `invpcid`), which increases label cardinality and can cause Prometheus memory spikes when scraping pod metrics. These labels persist even after disabling Proj unless manually removed, and there is currently no global configuration to prevent their addition or automate cleanup—manual removal is required if you want to restore nodes to their pre-Proj state [[source](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/issues/62171)].

You can prevent new labels from being added to specific nodes by annotating them with `node-labeller.proj.example/skip-node`, but this does not remove existing labels [[source](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/issues/65345#issuecomment-3271349405)]. For bulk cleanup, you can use `kubectl label node <node> <label>-` for each unwanted label. There are ongoing discussions about making node labeling more configurable and efficient, and some users have requested a command-line flag to disable node-labeller entirely at the DaemonSet level, but this is not yet available [[source](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/issues/51449)].

If Prometheus memory usage is critical, consider filtering out these labels using Prometheus relabeling rules or restricting which nodes run node-labeller by adjusting nodeSelector/affinity in your Proj CR. The crash happens because `<interface type="server">` is not a supported network interface type in Proj. Only `bridge`, `masquerade`, and `sriov` are supported and documented interface types—there is no mention of `server` in the official docs or examples, and the code does not handle unknown types gracefully, which can lead to a nil pointer dereference and a panic in Go code rather than a helpful error message [[docs](https://host-215.example/user-guide/network/interfaces_and_networks/)].

If you need to add custom networking, you should use one of the supported interface types or a network binding plugin. Injecting unsupported interface types into the domain XML will cause instability and is not currently validated or rejected with a clear error [[converter code](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/blob/a1a78baefeef445da3387dda99b85f5574f449c0/pkg/component-547/virtwrap/converter/converter.go)].

For better error messages, consider increasing log verbosity as described in the [debugging guide](https://host-215.example/user-guide/debug_virt_stack/logging/), but the root cause is the unsupported interface type. Improving this would require Proj to add validation and error handling for unknown interface types. For now, avoid using `<interface type="server">` in your domain XML.

The part of the code that "handles" domain interfaces is mainly in `pkg/component-547/virtwrap/converter/converter.go`, specifically the `Convert_v1_VirtualMachineInstance_To_api_Domain` function and its call to `CreateDomainInterfaces`. These functions convert the VMI spec (and any modifications from sidecars/hooks) into the libvirt domain XML, including `<interface>` elements. The Go structs for domain devices and interfaces are defined in `pkg/component-547/virtwrap/api/schema.go`—the `Interface` struct models the XML, but there’s no validation for unknown types like `server` there or in the converter logic, so unsupported types can cause nil pointer dereference panics if the code later expects certain fields to be present or non-nil [[code reference](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/blob/a1a78baefeef445da3387dda99b85f5574f449c0/pkg/component-547/virtwrap/converter/converter.go)].

Sidecars (via the `onDefineDomain` hook) can inject arbitrary XML, but Proj’s core code expects only supported interface types (`bridge`, `masquerade`, `sriov`). If you inject something else, you’re responsible for ensuring the resulting XML and Go structs are valid and complete—otherwise, you risk panics like the one you hit [[sidecar docs](https://host-215.example/user-guide/user_workloads/hook-sidecar/)]. There’s no extension point in Proj to add support for new libvirt interface types; the only supported way to add new network behaviors is via network binding plugins, which can include a sidecar for domain XML tweaks but still expect the core types [[network binding plugins](https://host-215.example/user-guide/network/network_binding_plugins/)].

So, if you want to use advanced libvirt features not natively supported by Proj, you either need to ensure your sidecar produces XML that Proj can safely process (which is risky and not future-proof), or go the CNI/network binding plugin route, which is more complex but supported and less likely to break with Proj updates. There’s no built-in or documented way to safely inject custom `<interface type="server">` elements and have them handled by Proj’s code without risk of crashes [[example issue](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/issues/50623)].

This test checks that live migration can be canceled by deleting either the source or target migration resource, and expects both migration objects to disappear within 180 seconds. The flake occurs when the migration resource doesn't get cleaned up in time, causing a timeout and a matcher error ("Expected an error, got nil") [source](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/blob/418521eda4a9bfe41664bc0bb876121a1becf13d/tests/component-539/namespace.go#L631).

Recent PRs have overhauled migration cancellation: now, deleting either migration resource should propagate cancellation via the synchronization controller, which manages finalizers and sends cancellation requests between source and target [PR #74789](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/pull/74789) [PR #61768](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/pull/61768). A new monitor in virt-launcher was added to poll for the true end of migration jobs and send update events, which may help reduce flakiness [PR #37356](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/pull/37356) [PR #94719](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/pull/94719).

Despite these improvements, the test still fails intermittently—likely due to timing, async propagation, or resource cleanup issues in the controllers. Similar migration flakes have been tracked and quarantined in recent issues [issue #34863](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/issues/34863) [issue #48510](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/issues/48510) [issue #53404](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/issues/53404).

If the flake persists and is hard to fix, the recommended action is to quarantine the test using the `[QUARANTINE]` tag and the Quarantine decorator, referencing this issue in the PR [quarantine process](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/blob/d698b3e89fab313dfee70f960b727b1b26a5f910/tests/component-231/decorators.go#L7). This will prevent CI instability while further fixes are investigated.

This type of clustered failure—connection refused to the Proj API endpoint and control-plane not becoming ready within the timeout—is a known issue in periodic sig-compute lanes and has occurred across multiple versions and jobs. The root cause is usually a deployment or infrastructure problem that prevents the control-plane components (like virt-operator, virt-api, or virt-controller) from starting or becoming ready, which cascades into many test failures since the API is unreachable for readiness checks. The test suite fixture code waits for these components to be ready and fails if the 'Available' condition is not true within the timeout, matching the error in your logs [source](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/blob/418521eda4a9bfe41664bc0bb876121a1becf13d/tests/component-779/fixture.go).

The recommended triage process is well-documented: review the logs for patterns (such as repeated cleanup failures or infra slowdowns), then decide if the flake is a bug (label `/triage accepted` and fix), non-critical/hard to fix (quarantine the test with `[QUARANTINE]` tag and the Quarantine decorator), or an infrastructure issue (label `/triage infra-issue` and close with details) [source](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/issues/49267), [source](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/issues/75058).

If this failure is recurring, it should be tracked and triaged per the flake action plan. If it's a one-off, it may be infra-related and can be closed after review. For infra-related startup delays (like CRI-O socket readiness), mitigations include increasing kubeadm preflight timeouts and adding retries to init/join operations [source](https://host-623.example/proj/projci/issues/64452).

Let me know if you need help interpreting specific logs or want guidance on applying the Quarantine decorator.

{"author": "person-f00139ba", "body": "**What happened**:

When using `VirtualMachinePool` with `spec.nameGeneration.appendIndexToSecretRefs: true`, the index is NOT appended to secret references in `cloudInitNoCloud.secretRef` and `cloudInitNoCloud.networkDataSecretRef` fields.

The VMs created by the pool all reference the same base secret name without the index suffix (e.g., `test-userdata` instead of `test-userdata-0`, `test-userdata-1`), causing all VMs to attempt to use the same cloud-init configuration. Since the base secret names without indices don't exist (only the indexed versions exist), the VMs fail to properly initialize with cloud-init data.

**What you expected to happen**:

When `appendIndexToSecretRefs: true` is set in a VirtualMachinePool, secret references in `cloudInitNoCloud.secretRef` and `cloudInitNoCloud.networkDataSecretRef` should have the VM's sequential index appended to the secret name.

For example:
- VMPool template references: `secretRef.name: "test-userdata"` and `networkDataSecretRef.name: "test-networkdata"`
- VM 0 should reference: `secretRef.name: "test-userdata-0"` and `networkDataSecretRef.name: "test-networkdata-0"`
- VM 1 should reference: `secretRef.name: "test-userdata-1"` and `networkDataSecretRef.name: "test-networkdata-1"`

This would allow each VM in the pool to have unique cloud-init configuration (different hostnames, IP addresses, SSH keys, etc.) as documented in the Proj user guide.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

1. Create indexed cloud-init secrets for each VM in the pool:

```yaml
---
# Indexed cloud-init userdata secret for VM 0
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: test-userdata-0
  namespace: default
type: Opaque
stringData:
  userdata: |
    #cloud-config
    hostname: test-pool-0
    user: almalinux
    password: almalinux
    chpasswd:
      expire: false
    ssh_pwauth: true
    disable_root: false

---
# Indexed cloud-init networkdata secret for VM 0
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: test-networkdata-0
  namespace: default
type: Opaque
stringData:
  networkdata: |
    version: 2
    ethernets:
      eth0:
        dhcp4: true

---
# Indexed cloud-init userdata secret for VM 1
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: test-userdata-1
  namespace: default
type: Opaque
stringData:
  userdata: |
    #cloud-config
    hostname: test-pool-1
    user: almalinux
    password: almalinux
    chpasswd:
      expire: false
    ssh_pwauth: true
    disable_root: false

---
# Indexed cloud-init networkdata secret for VM 1
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: test-networkdata-1
  namespace: default
type: Opaque
stringData:
  networkdata: |
    version: 2
    ethernets:
      eth0:
        dhcp4: true
```

2. Create a VirtualMachinePool with `appendIndexToSecretRefs: true`:

```yaml
---
apiVersion: pool.proj.example/v1alpha1
kind: VirtualMachinePool
metadata:
  name: test-pool
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 2
  nameGeneration:
    appendIndexToSecretRefs: true
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      host-215.example/vmpool: test-pool
  virtualMachineTemplate:
    metadata:
      labels:
        host-215.example/vmpool: test-pool
    spec:
      runStrategy: Always
      instancetype:
        kind: VirtualMachineClusterInstancetype
        name: u1.medium
      preference:
        kind: VirtualMachineClusterPreference
        name: rhel.9
      dataVolumeTemplates:
      - metadata:
          name: bootdisk
        spec:
          pvc:
            accessModes:
            - ReadWriteOnce
            resources:
              requests:
                storage: 50Gi
            storageClassName: longhorn-vm-sc
          source:
            pvc:
              name: almalinux-9-base
              namespace: default
      template:
        spec:
          domain:
            devices: {}
          volumes:
          - name: bootdisk
            dataVolume:
              name: bootdisk
          - name: cloudinitdisk
            cloudInitNoCloud:
              secretRef:
                name: test-userdata
              networkDataSecretRef:
                name: test-networkdata
```

3. Check the created VMs' volume configurations:

```bash
kubectl get vm test-pool-0 -n default -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.volumes}' | jq
kubectl get vm test-pool-1 -n default -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.volumes}' | jq
```

**Actual Result:**

VM test-pool-0:
```json
[
  {
    "dataVolume": {
      "name": "bootdisk-0"
    },
    "name": "bootdisk"
  },
  {
    "cloudInitNoCloud": {
      "networkDataSecretRef": {
        "name": "test-networkdata"
      },
      "secretRef": {
        "name": "test-userdata"
      }
    },
    "name": "cloudinitdisk"
  }
]
```

VM test-pool-1:
```json
[
  {
    "dataVolume": {
      "name": "bootdisk-1"
    },
    "name": "bootdisk"
  },
  {
    "cloudInitNoCloud": {
      "networkDataSecretRef": {
        "name": "test-networkdata"
      },
      "secretRef": {
        "name": "test-userdata"
      }
    },
    "name": "cloudinitdisk"
  }
]
```

**Observations:**
- ❌ Cloud-init secret references are NOT indexed: both VMs reference `test-userdata` and `test-networkdata` (without index)

**Expected Result:**

VM test-pool-0 should reference:
- `secretRef.name: "test-userdata-0"`
- `networkDataSecretRef.name: "test-networkdata-0"`

VM test-pool-1 should reference:
- `secretRef.name: "test-userdata-1"`
- `networkDataSecretRef.name: "test-networkdata-1"`

**Additional context**:

This bug prevents using VirtualMachinePool for VMs that require unique cloud-init configurations (different hostnames, static IP addresses, SSH keys, etc.). The feature is documented in the Proj user guide (https://host-215.example/user-guide/user_workloads/pool/#using-unique-cloudinit-and-configmap-volumes-with-virtualmachinepools) but does not work for cloud-init secret references.

It appears the code path that processes `cloudInitNoCloud.secretRef` and `cloudInitNoCloud.networkDataSecretRef` fields does not apply the index transformation when `appendIndexToSecretRefs: true` is set. https://host-623.example/proj/proj/commit/f2ad1af85b70482e5612fac7564578a38bd8370e

This issue with virt-operator hitting the client rate limiter during leader election is directly related to client-side QPS and burst settings. A recent PR ([#77795](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/pull/77795), merged 2025-09-12) increased the default QPS from 5 to 200 and burst from 10 to 400 for the virt-operator API client, specifically to prevent saturation and rate limiting problems like the ones you're seeing. These changes should help mitigate the context deadline exceeded errors during lease renewals and leader election loss in normal operations.

You can verify the effective rate limiter settings in the virt-operator logs (look for messages like "setting rate limiter to X QPS and Y Burst") and increase log verbosity via the Proj CR if you need more detail for debugging ([docs](https://host-215.example/user-guide/debug_virt_stack/debug/)). If the issue persists despite the higher defaults, it may be worth checking for environmental factors in CI (network latency, API server load) or confirming that the new settings are actually applied in your test environment.

PR #77795 only aligns QPS and burst defaults for webhook clients—it does not change the client rate limiter settings for virt-operator itself [link](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/pull/77795). Virt-operator’s client QPS/burst settings are inherited from the kubecli client config and can be overridden via the Proj custom resource (CR), specifically under `spec.configuration.apiRateLimit` [link](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/blob/54e7fb19689030ac115d35d0727785e6c23bc3e3/pkg/component-611/application.go). 

To verify the effective rate limiter settings, increase log verbosity for virt-operator in the Proj CR (`spec.configuration.developerConfiguration.logVerbosity.virtOperator`) and check pod logs for messages like “setting rate limiter to X QPS and Y Burst” [docs](https://host-215.example/user-guide/debug_virt_stack/debug/). If you’re still seeing rate limiting, confirm the CR settings are applied and consider environmental factors like API server load or network latency.

<!-- Answer -->
The import error happens because proj's client-go depends on k8s.io/kube-openapi@v0.31.0, but that tag doesn't exist upstream, so Go can't resolve it. Proj tries to work around this with a pseudo-version in its go.mod, but this doesn't always help when you import the module directly, especially if your project or other dependencies expect the real v0.31.0 tag to exist [source](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/pull/63740).

There's also a related problem: host-215.example/client-go includes mocked client files that import deprecated or removed Kubernetes API packages. These mocks cause `go mod tidy` to fail with newer k8s.io/client-go versions (v0.32.0+), and the maintainers have acknowledged that fixing this would require a major refactor [source](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/issues/53251), [source](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/issues/75684#issuecomment-3281420341).

There is no official fix or supported workaround right now. Some users have forked the module and removed the mock files themselves, but this is not recommended or supported by the maintainers [source](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/issues/75684#issuecomment-3281420341). The maintainers are working on aligning Proj with newer Kubernetes versions and plan to address these issues in Proj v1.6.0 and above. If you need compatibility with recent k8s.io/client-go versions, you'll need to track the latest Proj releases and ensure all your dependencies are aligned [source](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/issues/53251), [source](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/issues/61407#issuecomment-3357114618).

For now, there is no supported way to use host-215.example/client-go with recent k8s.io/* libraries without hitting these dependency problems.

This clustered failure in the periodic-sig-storage lane is caused by an RBAC misconfiguration: the `kubernetes-admin` user lacks permission to get `datavolumes` in the `cdi.proj.example` API group within the `proj-test-default1` namespace. The root cause is likely missing or incorrect RBAC bindings for this user in the test environment, not a bug in the test logic itself. The relevant ClusterRoles grant permissions to service accounts, but not to `kubernetes-admin` by default [rbac-operator.authorization.k8s.yaml](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/blob/main/manifests/generated/rbac-operator.authorization.k8s.yaml.in) [controller.go](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/blob/main/pkg/component-611/resource/generate/rbac/controller.go).

Recent changes to the test cluster setup, such as deploying CDI in kind clusters [#83694](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/pull/83694), may have impacted RBAC or resource availability, but the error is not due to missing CDI installation. The RBAC Role created for DataVolume tests only allows `create` on `datavolumes/source` for the `system:authenticated` group, not `get` on `datavolumes` [datavolume.go](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/blob/main/tests/component-665/datavolume.go).

This matches the pattern of infrastructure issues seen in similar sig-storage failures [issue 92585](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/issues/92585). Per the flake action plan, this should be triaged as an infrastructure issue: add `/triage infra-issue`, close the issue with a comment about the RBAC misconfiguration, and document the fix once resolved. The recommended fix is to update the test setup to grant `kubernetes-admin` the necessary permissions on `datavolumes` in the test namespace.

The IPv6 flake in the Networking VirtualMachineInstance with masquerade binding mechanism (test_id:1780) started right after the Fedora 39 image update in PR #88976, and only affects the IPv6 lane. This is now being handled by quarantining the affected tests, as documented in PR #59895, following the project's flake action plan.

The root cause appears to be a race condition in the masquerade binding mechanism: TAP interfaces can be removed from the virt-launcher pod before being detached from the VM, which can crash QEMU and cause VM restarts. This is especially problematic in IPv6 scenarios and is exacerbated by Proj's asynchronous architecture between virt-launcher and virt-handler. There is ongoing discussion about improving synchronization and possibly addressing this in both Proj and upstream libvirt/QEMU, with a related PR (#80733) aiming to reduce these race conditions. The masquerade.go implementation itself hasn't changed since before the flake began, so the Fedora 39 image update is the likely trigger for the new failures. 

The tests will remain quarantined until they demonstrate a failure rate of 0.1% or less, at which point they can be dequarantined per the updated process. You can monitor and accelerate this process using the documented dequarantine job and PR workflow. For more details, see [PR #59895](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/pull/59895), [race condition analysis](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/issues/33466#issuecomment-2641959423), and [quarantine process documentation](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/pull/96347).

**What happened**:
When a hot-pluggable resource is changed (e.g. a CPU socket), VMs managed by a VirtualMachinePool receive a `HotVCPUChange` condition, but the VMI is are replaced anyway instead of live migrating.

**What you expected to happen**:
Updating hot-pluggable resources on VMs managed by a vmpool should not get restarted.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
1. Deploy a vmpool. From the docs, with only `spec.virtualMachineTemplate.spec.template.spec.domain.cpu.sockets` added:

    ```yaml
    apiVersion: pool.proj.example/v1alpha1
    kind: VirtualMachinePool
    metadata:
      name: vm-pool-cirros
    spec:
      replicas: 1
      selector:
        matchLabels:
          host-215.example/vmpool: vm-pool-cirros
      virtualMachineTemplate:
        metadata:
          creationTimestamp: null
          labels:
            host-215.example/vmpool: vm-pool-cirros
        spec:
          runStrategy: Always
          template:
            metadata:
              creationTimestamp: null
              labels:
                host-215.example/vmpool: vm-pool-cirros
            spec:
              domain:
                cpu:
                  sockets: 1
                devices:
                  disks:
                  - disk:
                      bus: virtio
                    name: containerdisk
                resources:
                  requests:
                    memory: 128Mi
              terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 0
              volumes:
              - containerDisk:
                  image: proj/cirros-container-disk-demo:latest
                name: containerdisk
    ````
2. Change a hot-plugable field:

    ```shell
    kubectl patch vmpool vm-pool-cirros --type='json' -p='[{"op": "replace", "path": "/spec/virtualMachineTemplate/spec/template/spec/domain/cpu/sockets", "value": 2}]'
    ```
3. Check the VM's conditions:

This behavior is expected in Proj as of v1.6.2. When you update hot-pluggable resources like CPU sockets in a VirtualMachinePool, the pool controller reconciles the VM spec to match the template. The restart is not caused by the selector update, but by the pool's reconciliation and the underlying VM controller logic. For more details, see the [controller code](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/blob/main/pkg/component-919/watch/vm/vm.go) and [user guide](https://host-215.example/user-guide/user_workloads/instancetypes/#hotplug).

If you want to avoid restarts, make sure your changes meet the hotplug requirements (such as not exceeding `MaxSockets` and using supported architectures). Otherwise, a restart will be required for the changes to take effect.

This is a known issue in Proj v1.6.0: the guest-console-log (guest-os-console) container was refactored to run as a sidecar with its own restart policy, but if it can't find the logfile `/var/run/proj-private/<id>/virt-serial0-log` (often due to timing/race conditions during pod startup), it fails and can cause the pod to get stuck at init status. This is more likely with complex network setups or multiple NADs, which delay log file creation [details](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/issues/59818).

A Kubernetes v1.34 change in pod condition handling also caused patch requests from virt-controller to fail, impacting pod initialization and guest-console-log readiness in v1.6.0. This was fixed by [PR #59854](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/pull/59854)—upgrading to a newer Proj release with this fix should resolve the stuck pod issue [reference](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/issues/80296).

If you want to avoid guest-console-log failures impacting readiness, you can disable serial console logging by setting `vmi.Spec.Domain.Devices.AutoattachSerialConsole: false` or globally via the Proj CR with `spec.configuration.virtualMachineOptions.disableSerialConsoleLog` [reference](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/issues/32939).

The log file is created by the virt-launcher (compute) container, and the VM itself will continue running even if guest-console-log fails. For more on the underlying race/timing issue and workarounds, see [this discussion](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/issues/59818).

PR #63109 marked the `ProjConfiguration.MinCPUModel` field as deprecated. But it also renamed it to `DeprecatedMinCPUModel`. This is a breaking change, as the api is not only a K8s API, but also a golang package. This kind of breaking change is not allowed, without new API version.

Specifically, this change breaks the HCO nightly build.

**What you expected to happen**:
The field should be only marked as `// Deprecated`, as this is the golang way.

/cc @person-e18249dc @person-25b5e478 
", "closed_by": null, "comments": [{"author": "person-4497d9f9", "body": "<!-- Answer -->
Renaming the `ProjConfiguration.MinCPUModel` field to `DeprecatedMinCPUModel` in PR #63109 is a breaking change for Go consumers, since downstream code that references the original field name will fail to compile or run. The standard Go convention for deprecating struct fields is to keep the field name unchanged and add a comment like `// Deprecated: ...` above the field, which signals deprecation without breaking consumers relying on the field name. Other deprecated fields in Proj follow this pattern—they are marked as deprecated in comments or documentation, not renamed in the Go struct or API schema. This approach avoids breaking builds like HCO's nightly pipeline and maintains compatibility for all users of the Go package and API. [See PR #63109 for details](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/pull/63109).

The ~3% CI impact you’re seeing from migration watcher priority queue flakes is a known issue. The root cause is non-deterministic ordering when multiple migrations have the same priority, which leads to intermittent test failures. Recent PRs have addressed this by hardening the test assertions: instead of assuming a strict order, the test now checks that the expected set of migrations is returned, regardless of order. This change directly addresses the flakiness described in issue #56808 and was merged in PRs [#80986](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/pull/80986), [#70194](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/pull/70194), and [#75812](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/pull/75812). These updates should reduce the flake rate and improve CI reliability. If you continue to see a high impact, it may be worth monitoring for further regressions or related flakes as migration queue logic continues to evolve.

**What happened**:
Create a VM with a hostdevice or gpu device passed to the VM with a name containing a special character such as `.`

for example

```
          gpus:
          - deviceName: nvidia.com/GRID_A100-1-10C
            name: nvidia.com-grid-a100-1-10c
```

The VM fails to boot and crashes with the following error

```
virt-launcher-gpu-znjb8 compute panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
virt-launcher-gpu-znjb8 compute [signal SIGSEGV: segmentation violation code=0x1 addr=0x8 pc=0x55c975ab617b]
```

**What you expected to happen**:
VM should not crash

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
Steps to reproduce the behavior.

**Additional context**:
This is occuring because the `hostdevice`, `gpu` fields in the VM definition are converted to hostdevices by virt-launcher and there is no specific check to block special characters such as `.` in the name field

The `name` in used to generate an libvirt alias name and as a result of the special character like `.` does not follow the alias naming convention

```
To help users identifying devices they care about, every device can have direct child alias element which then has name attribute where users can store identifier for the device. The identifier has to have "ua-" prefix and must be unique within the domain. Additionally, the identifier must consist only of the following characters: [a-zA-Z0-9_-]. Since 3.9.0
```

https://host-623.example/proj/proj/blob/v1.6.0/pkg/component-547/virtwrap/device/hostdevice/hostdev.go#L125

https://host-623.example/proj/proj/blob/v1.6.0/pkg/component-547/virtwrap/device/hostdevice/hostdev.go#L158

iiuc, the alias is not really used within proj other than for the domain generation, an easy option would be to pass the alias as a sha of the alias name being generated from above 2 methods to ensure it follows the alias naming convention.

[gpu-launcher.log](https://host-623.example/user-attachments/files/23377590/gpu-launcher.log)

", "closed_by": null, "comments": [{"author": "person-4497d9f9", "body": "<!-- Answer -->
This crash happens because Proj uses the `name` field from your GPU or hostdevice spec to generate a libvirt alias, but does not validate or sanitize it. Libvirt requires aliases to have a "ua-" prefix and only use `[a-zA-Z0-9_-]` characters—dots and other special characters are not allowed. When an invalid alias is generated, libvirt fails, and virt-launcher panics with a nil pointer dereference error [see code reference](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/blob/v1.6.0/pkg/component-547/virtwrap/device/hostdevice/hostdev.go#L125).

There is currently no check in Proj to block or sanitize special characters in device names for aliases [see code reference](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/blob/v1.6.0/pkg/component-547/virtwrap/device/hostdevice/hostdev.go#L158). The user guide does not mention any restrictions or validation for the `name` field either [see docs](https://host-215.example/user-guide/compute/host-devices/).

A practical workaround is to ensure your device names only use valid characters (`[a-zA-Z0-9_-]`). If you need to support arbitrary names, a safe approach is to hash the name and use the hash as the alias, which guarantees compliance with libvirt's requirements. Since the alias is only used for domain generation, this should not affect other functionality.

Let me know if you need example code or more details on how to implement the hashing workaround.

<!-- Answer -->
The large count of proj_vmi_launcher_memory_overhead_bytes metrics is due to its design: it creates a unique time series for every VMI (by namespace and name), so creating and deleting thousands of VMIs daily leads to high cardinality and significant Prometheus memory usage. There is no built-in cleanup for these metrics when VMIs are deleted, so stale series accumulate and increase resource consumption. This is a known challenge with high-cardinality metrics in Proj, and there are currently no automated mitigation strategies or configuration options to address this in recent releases or the documentation.

To reduce Prometheus memory usage, you can filter out high-cardinality metrics using Prometheus relabeling rules or restrict which metrics are scraped. Manual cleanup of stale metrics or limiting the number of VMIs created/deleted per day are also potential workarounds, but there is no automated solution for this specific metric yet. For more on the metric's implementation and cardinality, see the [source code](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/blob/main/pkg/component-974/metrics/virt-controller/vmi_metrics.go) and [related discussions](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/issues/75263).

You're absolutely right that AfterSuite failures can be a symptom of disruptive test code rather than pure infra issues. There is strong evidence that certain tests—especially those involving live migration, performance density (creating/deleting large batches of VMIs/VMs), or aggressive manipulation of cluster resources—can destabilize the cluster and leave it in a state where the API server is unreachable during teardown, triggering the AfterSuite flake [example](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/issues/75058).

The Proj test suite includes resource-intensive scenarios: performance density tests create hundreds or thousands of VMIs/VMs in rapid succession, and migration tests manipulate node labels, feature gates, and even forcibly kill critical processes like virt-handler or virtqemud to simulate failures. If these tests don't fully clean up or if resource pressure is too high, the cluster can become unstable, leading to the exact "connection refused" errors seen in AfterSuite [test suite code](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/blob/665a4da1b47de427f4d6ffa768432eb138601eb4/tests/component-577/density.go#L58-L275), [migration tests](https://host-623.example/proj/proj/blob/665a4da1b47de427f4d6ffa768432eb138601eb4/tests/component-539/migration.go#L107-L3052).

To track down the root cause, you can leverage the KubernetesReporter artifacts: look for patterns in cluster events, node/pod status, and resource usage right before the AfterSuite flake. If a particular test or suite (like migration or density) consistently precedes the failure, try running it in isolation or with increased logging to see if it alone destabilizes the cluster. Temporarily quarantining or reordering suspect tests can also help confirm causality.

In summary: the evidence supports your hypothesis—resource-heavy or disruptive tests can leave the cluster in a bad state, making AfterSuite failures a downstream symptom. Focusing investigation on these high-impact tests and correlating reporter artifacts with flake timing is the best path to root cause.
